notes.title: Computer basics, memory hierarchy, OS, CPU cycle
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- CPU = ALU + control unit + registers.
- Memory hierarchy: registers → cache → RAM → disk.
- Cycle: fetch → decode → execute.

---

## Anatomy of a computer (Von Neumann)
Input → **CPU** (ALU + Control Unit + registers) ↔ **Memory** → Output, connected by buses (address, data, control).

## Classification
By size: micro, mini, mainframe, supercomputer. By data: analog, digital, hybrid. By purpose: general, special.

## Memory hierarchy (fast/small/costly at the top)
Registers → Cache (L1/L2/L3) → Main memory (RAM) → Secondary (SSD/HDD) → Tertiary (tape, optical).
Going down: **speed ↓, capacity ↑, cost per bit ↓**. Primary memory is volatile (RAM) or non-volatile (ROM).

## Operating system
Software that manages hardware and provides services to programs: process management, memory management, file system, device (I/O) management, security, user interface. Types: batch, multiprogramming, time-sharing, real-time, distributed.

## CPU operation: the instruction cycle
**Fetch** (PC → MAR, memory → MDR → IR, PC + 1) → **Decode** (the control unit interprets the opcode) → **Execute** (the ALU operates, the result goes to a register or memory) → repeat.

notes.title: Programming languages; compile, link, load
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- 1GL machine, 2GL assembly, 3GL high-level (C).
- Compiler: whole program at once. Interpreter: line by line.
- Pipeline: preprocess → compile → assemble → link → load.

---

## Generations
| Gen | Language | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1GL | Machine (binary) | fast, hardware-specific |
| 2GL | Assembly (mnemonics) | needs an assembler |
| 3GL | High-level: C, Java | portable, needs a compiler or interpreter |
| 4GL | SQL, MATLAB | closer to the problem |
| 5GL | Prolog | declarative, AI |

Classification: low-level vs high-level; procedural (C), object-oriented (Java), functional, logic.

## Compiler vs interpreter
| Compiler | Interpreter |
|---|---|
| translates the whole program at once | line by line |
| produces an object/executable file | no separate file |
| faster execution | slower execution |
| errors listed after compiling | stops at the first error |
| C, C++ | Python, BASIC |

## From source to running program
`prog.c` → **preprocessor** (`#include`, `#define`) → **compiler** → assembly → **assembler** → `prog.o` (object code) → **linker** (adds library code like `printf`, resolves references) → executable → **loader** (copies it into memory, sets the start address) → runs.

notes.title: Algorithms, pseudocode, flowcharts
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Algorithm = finite, clear steps with input and output.
- Three forms: steps, pseudocode, flowchart.
- Symbols: oval start/stop, parallelogram I/O, rectangle process, diamond decision.

---

## Algorithm
A finite, ordered set of unambiguous steps that solves a problem. **Properties:** input, output, definiteness, finiteness, effectiveness.

## Three ways to state it (sum of two numbers)
**Step form:** 1. Start 2. Read a, b 3. sum ← a + b 4. Print sum 5. Stop
**Pseudocode:** `BEGIN  READ a, b  SET sum = a + b  PRINT sum  END`
**Flowchart:** oval (Start) → parallelogram (Read a, b) → rectangle (sum = a + b) → parallelogram (Print sum) → oval (Stop)

## Flowchart symbols
| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Oval (terminal) | start / stop |
| Parallelogram | input / output |
| Rectangle | process |
| Diamond | decision (yes/no) |
| Arrow | flow |
| Circle | connector |

## Program development steps
Problem definition → analysis → algorithm/flowchart → coding → testing and debugging → documentation → maintenance.

**Exam favourites:** the largest of three numbers, whether n is prime, factorial, sum of digits — have each as an algorithm *and* a flowchart.

notes.title: Structured programming
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Only 3 structures: sequence, selection, iteration.
- Avoid goto: spaghetti code.
- Design top-down: split into sub-problems.

---

**Structured programming:** programs built from three control structures only, with single entry and single exit.
1. **Sequence**: statements one after another
2. **Selection**: if / if-else / switch
3. **Iteration**: while / do-while / for

(Böhm–Jacopini theorem: any algorithm can be written with these three.)

## Why `goto` is discouraged
It creates arbitrary jumps ("spaghetti code"), so you can't tell how a line is reached, and debugging and proving correctness get harder. Every use can be replaced by loops, `break` or functions.

## Algorithm design strategies
Top-down (stepwise refinement: split into sub-problems), bottom-up, divide and conquer, modular design (functions).

**Advantages of structured programming:** readable, easier to debug and test, maintainable, reusable modules.

notes.title: Structure of a C program
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Sections: docs, #include, #define, globals, main(), functions.
- Execution starts at main().
- return 0 means success.

---

```c
/* documentation: name, purpose */     // 1. Documentation
#include <stdio.h>                     // 2. Link (preprocessor)
#define PI 3.14                        // 3. Definition
int count = 0;                         // 4. Global declarations
int area(int r);                       //    function prototypes
int main(void) {                       // 5. main()
    int r = 2;                         //    declaration part
    printf("%d\n", area(r));           //    executable part
    return 0;                          //    0 = success, to the OS
}
int area(int r) { return PI * r * r; } // 6. Sub-programs
```
- Execution **always starts at `main()`**.
- Statements end with `;`. Blocks go in `{ }`.
- Comments: `/* multi-line */` and `// single line`. They're ignored by the compiler.
- `return 0;` from main reports successful termination.
- **Writing → running:** edit (`.c`) → compile (`gcc prog.c -o prog`) → run (`./prog`).

notes.title: C tokens, keywords, identifiers
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- 6 tokens: keywords, identifiers, constants, strings, operators, symbols.
- Identifiers: letters, digits, _; can't start with a digit.
- C has 32 keywords; C is case-sensitive.

---

**Token** = the smallest unit of a program. Six types:
| Token | Examples |
|---|---|
| Keywords | `int`, `return`, `while` (32 in C89) |
| Identifiers | `sum`, `_count`, `total2` |
| Constants | `10`, `3.14`, `'A'` |
| Strings | `"hello"` |
| Operators | `+ = == && ++` |
| Special symbols | `{ } ( ) [ ] ; , #` |

## Identifier rules
- Letters, digits, underscore only.
- Must **not start with a digit**.
- No keywords; no spaces or special characters.
- Case-sensitive (`Sum` ≠ `sum`).
Valid: `_temp`, `roll_no`, `x1`. Invalid: `2x`, `int`, `roll-no`, `my var`.

## The 32 keywords
auto break case char const continue default do double else enum extern float for goto if int long register return short signed sizeof static struct switch typedef union unsigned void volatile while

notes.title: Data types, variables, constants, operators
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- int 4 B %d, char 1 B %c, float 4 B %f, double 8 B %lf.
- % works only on integers.
- 5/2 = 2 (integer division).

---

## Basic types (typical 32/64-bit gcc)
| Type | Size | Range / precision | Format |
|---|---|---|---|
| `char` | 1 B | −128 to 127 | `%c` |
| `int` | 4 B | −2³¹ to 2³¹−1 (≈ ±2.1×10⁹) | `%d` |
| `short` | 2 B | −32768 to 32767 | `%hd` |
| `long` | 8 B (4 on Windows) | | `%ld` |
| `float` | 4 B | ~6–7 digits | `%f` |
| `double` | 8 B | ~15 digits | `%lf` |
Modifiers: `signed`, `unsigned`, `short`, `long`. `void` = no value.

## Constants
Integer (`10`, `012` octal, `0xA` hex), real (`3.14`, `1e-3`), character (`'A'`), string (`"A"` — two bytes, including `'\0'`), `const int x = 5;`, `#define N 10`.

## Operators
| Category | Operators |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` (`%` is integers only) |
| Relational | `< > <= >= == !=` (give 1 or 0) |
| Logical | `&& || !` (short-circuit) |
| Assignment | `= += -= *= /= %=` |
| Increment/decrement | `++ --` (prefix changes then uses; postfix uses then changes) |
| Bitwise | `& | ^ ~ << >>` |
| Conditional | `?:` |
| Special | `sizeof`, `,`, `&` (address), `*` |

**Traps:** `5/2 = 2` (integer division); `-7 % 3 = -1` (the sign follows the dividend); `'A' + 1 = 66`.

notes.title: Precedence, associativity, type conversion
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- * / % before + −, then relational, ==, &&, ||, ?:, =.
- Unary, ?: and = go right to left.
- Mixed types promote up: int → float → double.

---

## Precedence (high → low)
| Level | Operators | Associativity |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `() [] -> .` postfix `++ --` | L → R |
| 2 | unary `+ - ! ~` prefix `++ --` `(type)` `*` `&` `sizeof` | **R → L** |
| 3 | `* / %` | L → R |
| 4 | `+ -` | L → R |
| 5 | `<< >>` | L → R |
| 6 | `< <= > >=` | L → R |
| 7 | `== !=` | L → R |
| 8–10 | `&` then `^` then `|` | L → R |
| 11–12 | `&&` then `||` | L → R |
| 13 | `?:` | **R → L** |
| 14 | `= += -=` … | **R → L** |
| 15 | `,` | L → R |

## Type conversion
- **Implicit (promotion):** char/short → int; in mixed expressions the lower type converts to the higher: int → long → float → double.
- **Explicit (cast):** `(float)a / b`.
- Assigning a float to an int **truncates**: `int x = 3.9;` gives 3.

## Worked
`int a = 5, b = 2; float c = a / b;` → **2.000000** (integer division happens first). `(float)a / b` → 2.5.
`x = 10 + 3 * 2 - 8 / 4 % 3;` → `10 + 6 - (2 % 3)` = `16 - 2` = **14**.

**Trap:** `i++ + ++i` modifies `i` twice without a sequence point: **undefined behaviour**. Say so in the answer if it's asked.

notes.title: Input/output functions and escape sequences
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- scanf needs & before variables.
- %.2f = 2 decimals, %5d = width 5.
- Use " %c" to skip the leftover newline.

---

## Formatted I/O
`printf("format", args)`, `scanf("format", &vars)` — scanf needs the **address** `&` (except for strings/arrays).
Specifiers: `%d %i %u %ld %f %lf %e %c %s %x %o %p %%`
Width and precision: `%5d` (right-aligned in 5), `%-5d` (left), `%.2f` (2 decimals), `%8.3f`, `%05d` (zero-padded).

## Unformatted I/O
`getchar()` / `putchar(c)` — one character. `gets()` (unsafe, removed in C11) / `puts(s)` (adds a newline). Use `fgets(s, n, stdin)`.

## The scanf newline trap
`scanf("%d", &n); scanf("%c", &ch);` → `ch` receives the leftover `'\n'`. Fix: `scanf(" %c", &ch);` — the leading space skips whitespace.

## Escape sequences
| Seq | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\n` | newline |
| `\t` | tab |
| `\\` | backslash |
| `\"` | double quote |
| `\'` | single quote |
| `\0` | null character |
| `\a` | bell |
| `\b` | backspace |
| `\r` | carriage return |

`printf` returns the number of characters printed: `printf("%d", printf("hi"));` prints `hi2`.

notes.title: if and if-else
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Non-zero = true, 0 = false.
- = assigns, == compares (classic bug).
- A ; right after if() ends the if.

---

```c
if (condition) { ... }
if (condition) { ... } else { ... }
if (c1) {...} else if (c2) {...} else {...}   // else-if ladder
```
- Any non-zero value is true; 0 is false.
- Without braces, only **one statement** belongs to the if.

## Classic traps
- `if (x = 5)` **assigns** 5, so it's always true. Use `==`. (Writing `5 == x` makes the compiler catch the mistake.)
- `if (x > 0);` — the stray semicolon makes the body empty.
- Comparing floats with `==`: use `fabs(a - b) < 1e-9`.

## Standard programs
Even/odd (`n % 2 == 0`), largest of two or three, leap year (`(y % 4 == 0 && y % 100 != 0) || y % 400 == 0`), grade from marks (else-if ladder), positive/negative/zero.

notes.title: Nested if and the conditional operator
switch and the comma operator
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- switch works on int/char only.
- No break → falls into the next case.
- default runs when no case matches.

---

```c
switch (expr) {           // expr: int or char only (no float, no strings)
  case 1:  ...; break;
  case 2:  ...; break;
  default: ...;           // optional; any position
}
```
- Case labels must be **constant** and **unique** integers or characters.
- **Fall-through:** without `break`, execution continues into the next case. It can be used on purpose to group cases: `case 'a': case 'e': ... vowel`.
- `default` runs when nothing matches.

**switch vs else-if ladder:** switch tests only equality on an integer or char, and is cleaner for menus. if-else handles ranges, floats and complex conditions.

## Comma operator
Evaluates left to right; the value is the **last** expression. `x = (a = 2, a + 3);` → x = 5. Common in `for (i = 0, j = n; i < j; i++, j--)`.

**Output trap:** `int x = 2; switch (x) { case 1: printf("1"); case 2: printf("2"); case 3: printf("3"); }` → prints **23** (fall-through).

notes.title: while and do-while
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- while checks first (may run 0 times).
- do-while checks last (runs at least once).
- do-while ends with ;

---

```c
while (cond) { body; }            // entry-controlled: may run 0 times
do { body; } while (cond);        // exit-controlled: runs at least once — note the ;
```
**The one real difference:** do-while checks **after** the body, so it always runs at least once (useful for menus and input validation).

## Standard programs
- Sum of digits / reverse a number: `while (n > 0) { d = n % 10; sum += d; rev = rev * 10 + d; n /= 10; }`
- Palindrome number, Armstrong number (sum of the cubes of the digits = n for 3 digits), GCD (Euclid: `while (b) { t = b; b = a % b; a = t; }`).

## Traps
- Forgetting to update the loop variable → infinite loop.
- `while (x < 10);` — the stray semicolon makes an empty body loop forever.
- `int i = 5; do { printf("%d", i); } while (i < 3);` → prints **5** once.

notes.title: for loop, break, continue, goto, return, exit
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- for(init; test; update).
- break leaves the loop; continue skips to the next round.
- exit() ends the program; return ends the function.

---

```c
for (init; condition; update) { body; }
```
Any part can be empty; `for (;;)` is an infinite loop. Order: init → test → body → update → test …

## Jump statements
| Statement | Effect |
|---|---|
| `break` | leaves the **innermost** loop or switch |
| `continue` | skips to the next iteration (in a `for`, the update still runs) |
| `goto label;` | jumps to a label in the same function (avoid) |
| `return` | leaves the current function (with a value) |
| `exit(n)` | ends the whole program (`<stdlib.h>`); 0 = success |

## Nested-loop patterns
```c
for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for (j = 1; j <= i; j++) printf("*"); printf("\n"); }
```
The outer loop is rows, the inner loop is what's printed per row.

## Output traps
- `for (i = 0; i < 5; i++); printf("%d", i);` → **5** (empty body).
- `for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) { if (i == 1) continue; printf("%d", i); }` → **02**.
- `for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) { if (i == 3) break; printf("%d", i); }` → **012**.

notes.title: Functions: types and parameter passing
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- Prototype, definition, call.
- 4 types by args/return.
- Call by value copies: a swap won't work without pointers.

---

```c
int add(int a, int b);                  // declaration (prototype)
int main(void) { int s = add(2, 3); }   // call: 2, 3 are the actual arguments
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } // definition: a, b are the formal parameters
```
**Why functions:** modularity, reuse, easier debugging, less repetition.

## Four types by arguments and return value
| Type | Example |
|---|---|
| No args, no return | `void greet(void)` |
| Args, no return | `void show(int n)` |
| No args, return | `int readNum(void)` |
| Args and return | `int add(int a, int b)` |

Library functions (`printf`, `sqrt`) vs user-defined functions.

## Parameter passing
- **Call by value** (C's default): a *copy* is passed, so changes inside don't affect the caller.
- **Call by reference** (using pointers): pass the address, `swap(&a, &b)` with `void swap(int *x, int *y) { int t = *x; *x = *y; *y = t; }`, so the caller's variables change.

**Trap:** a swap written with call by value leaves the originals unchanged. That's the classic viva question.

notes.title: Recursion and call by value
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- A function calling itself.
- Needs a base case to stop.
- fact(n) = n × fact(n−1); Hanoi takes 2ⁿ−1 moves.

---

**Recursion:** a function that calls itself. It needs (1) a **base case** that stops and (2) a **recursive case** that moves toward the base.

```c
int fact(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * fact(n - 1); }
int fib(int n)  { if (n <= 1) return n; return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2); }
void hanoi(int n, char s, char d, char a) {
    if (n == 0) return;
    hanoi(n - 1, s, a, d); printf("%c->%c\n", s, d); hanoi(n - 1, a, d, s);
}   // 2^n - 1 moves
```
## Stack trace: fact(3)
fact(3) → 3 × fact(2) → 2 × fact(1) → returns 1 → 2 × 1 = 2 → 3 × 2 = **6**. Each call gets its own stack frame with its own copy of `n` (call by value).

| Recursion | Iteration |
|---|---|
| elegant for trees, Hanoi | usually faster |
| uses stack memory, can overflow | constant memory |
| base case essential | loop condition essential |

**Trap:** no base case (or one that's never reached) → infinite recursion → stack overflow.

notes.title: Storage classes
notes.content:
### ⚡ In 30 seconds
- auto: default, garbage, block scope.
- static: keeps its value between calls, default 0.
- extern: declared here, defined elsewhere. register: no &.

---

| Class | Storage | Default value | Scope | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `auto` | stack (memory) | garbage | block | until the block ends |
| `register` | CPU register (a request) | garbage | block | until the block ends |
| `static` (local) | data segment | **0** | block | **whole program** |
| `static` (global) | data segment | 0 | this file only | whole program |
| `extern` | data segment | 0 | global, across files | whole program |

- `auto` is the default for local variables.
- You **can't take `&`** of a `register` variable.
- A `static` local keeps its value between calls:
```c
void f(void) { static int c = 0; c++; printf("%d ", c); }   // f(); f(); f(); → 1 2 3
```
- `extern int x;` **declares** without allocating; the definition is in another file.

notes.title: C Unit 1 — one-page revision sheet
notes.content:
| Topic | Must know |
|---|---|
| Computer anatomy | Input, CPU (ALU, CU, registers), memory, output; buses |
| Memory hierarchy | registers → cache → RAM → secondary; speed ↓, size ↑, cost ↓ |
| OS | process, memory, file, device management |
| Instruction cycle | fetch (PC→MAR→MDR→IR), decode, execute |
| Language generations | 1GL machine … 5GL; compiler vs interpreter table |
| Build pipeline | preprocess → compile → assemble → link → load |
| Algorithms | properties; step form, pseudocode, flowchart; the symbols |
| Structured programming | sequence, selection, iteration; why no goto |

notes.title: C Unit 2 — one-page revision sheet
notes.content:
| Topic | Must know |
|---|---|
| Program structure | 6 sections; execution starts at main; return 0 |
| Tokens | 6 types; identifier rules; 32 keywords |
| Data types | sizes, ranges, format specifiers |
| Operators | categories; `%` integers only; pre vs post increment |
| Precedence | unary R→L, `*/%` > `+-` > relational > `==` > `&&` > `||` > `?:` > `=` |
| Conversion | implicit promotion; cast; `5/2 = 2` |

notes.title: C Unit 3 — one-page revision sheet
notes.content:
| Topic | Must know |
|---|---|
| I/O | specifiers, width/precision, `&` in scanf, the `" %c"` fix |
| if / else | `=` vs `==`, stray `;`, dangling else pairs with the nearest if |
| Ternary | `a > b ? a : b`; largest of three |
| switch | int/char, constant labels, fall-through without break |
| Loops | while (entry) vs do-while (exit, at least once) vs for |
| Jumps | break (innermost), continue (skip; for still updates), goto, return, exit |

**Output questions:** trace variables in a table, one row per iteration.

notes.title: C Unit 4 — one-page revision sheet
notes.content:
| Topic | Must know |
|---|---|
| Functions | prototype, definition, call; formal vs actual parameters; 4 types |
| Call by value | copies; swap fails. Call by reference: pointers; swap works |
| Recursion | base case + recursive case; stack trace; factorial, fibonacci, Hanoi ($2^n-1$ moves) |
| Storage classes | the 5-row table: storage, default, scope, lifetime; static keeps its value |

**Class Test 1 covers Units 3 and 4.**
